narrative:
The model predicted a 73% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is well above the acceptance threshold, your law school application was rejected.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors from your academic record. Your third-year class ranking had the strongest influence, pushing the prediction strongly toward failure. Placing in the 3rd decile is noticeably lower than the average 5.8 decile among students who were accepted, signaling that your later-year performance was weaker than most successful applicants. Your LSAT score was the second most important factor and also pulled the prediction toward failure; your score of 31 sits substantially below the 37-point average of accepted students. Finally, your undergraduate GPA of 2.7 contributed additional downward pressure, compared with an average of 3.23 among those who received offers.

None of these features pointed in a favorable direction. Together they created a clear picture for the model that your academic preparation made success on the bar exam less likely.

What you should do next is straightforward: strengthen the areas the model weighed most heavily. Retake the LSAT and aim for a meaningfully higher score, improve your study habits to raise your class ranking in future coursework, and consider a post-baccalaureate program or additional classes that can demonstrate a higher GPA. Once those numbers move closer to the accepted averages, reapply. Many students improve these exact metrics and gain admission on a later attempt.
